headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers: one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, each built from a single uploaded document, so nothing here describes either condition in general.

Both papers report that they do not measure indirect costs such as lost income, caregiving time, or productivity loss, and both flag a subgroup-disaggregation limitation in how their headline aggregate figures are broken down.

The two papers differ in how official data undercounts the condition studied: the Lyme disease paper relies on an unvalidated claims-based diagnosis algorithm, while the Long COVID paper notes no specific diagnostic code existed for the condition during its study period, so costs had to be inferred by proxy.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a patient out-of-pocket cost of $188 per episode overall (2022 dollars), rising to $401 per episode for disseminated disease, but notes this figure is only available for the 15.5% of case patients with OOP claims data.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper does not isolate out-of-pocket costs; its direct medical cost figures already combine payer- and patient-paid amounts, and the paper explicitly treats OOP burden as a separate, unestimated category.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper gives a reader a concrete out-of-pocket dollar figure to plan around.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports a disseminated-minus-localized direct cost difference of $6,138 per episode and a disseminated-to-localized cost ratio of 9.83 (2022 dollars for the dollar figure).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports a hospitalization cost multiplier of 3.18 for adults and 9.47 for children at 6 months (2020 dollars underlying the associated absolute differences).

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show that a more severe or hospitalized course of the condition studied is linked to a much larger direct cost than a milder course, even though the two papers use different metrics and price years that should not be compared as equal numbers.

comparison_rows.dimension: Work and income or productivity loss

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper states explicitly that its cost estimation 'does not include all states or indirect costs,' meaning lost income and caregiving time are not measured anywhere in the paper.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper explicitly lists productivity losses for patients or caregivers as not captured by its data.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper can speak to the income or caregiving burden of the condition it covers, so any work-loss claims would need a different kind of evidence.

comparison_rows.dimension: How official data undercounts the condition

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper identifies cases using ICD-10 diagnosis codes and an antibiotic-prescription algorithm that the authors themselves say 'may not be generalizable to all patients with LD,' and the localized/disseminated classification algorithm 'has not been validated.'

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper notes that no post-COVID-19-condition-specific ICD-10 code existed during its study period, so cases were inferred by comparing costs of diagnosed COVID-19 patients to matched controls, which the authors describe as producing a lower bound in the setting studied.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The two papers describe different mechanisms by which official claims data can produce lower or different counts in the setting studied: one is an unvalidated classification algorithm, the other is an absent diagnostic code.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's methods include the 30 days before diagnosis in the follow-up window to capture possible diagnostic-workup costs, implying a diagnostic-delay-related cost, but this is not separately quantified as its own figure.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper summary provided does not describe any diagnostic-delay cost measurement.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Lyme disease paper even gestures toward a diagnostic-delay cost, and even there it is not separately measured.

comparison_rows.dimension: Extrapolated or aggregate economic burden scope

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper extrapolates to an annual cost of $591,000,000-$1,050,000,000 across 16 high-incidence states and DC (2022 dollars), explicitly excluding other states and indirect costs.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports an aggregate cohort total of up to $47,000,000 for children and up to $308,000,000 for adults (2020 dollars), but states this applies only to its specific matched study cohort and is not a national or annual population-wide estimate.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: The Lyme disease paper offers a stated multi-state annual projection while the Long COVID paper's aggregate figure is explicitly scoped to one study cohort, so the two should not be read as comparable population-level totals.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's subgroup-disaggregation limitation notes that headline cost figures are reported by severity subgroup and state-incidence status but not disaggregated by sex, age group, race/ethnicity, disability, or other demographic subgroups.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's subgroup-disaggregation limitation notes that its cohort-level aggregate totals ($47 million children, $308 million adults) are presented as single pooled figures without demographic breakdown, even though per-person cost estimates elsewhere in the same paper were broken out by sex and age.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: In both papers, the biggest-picture dollar figures are the ones least broken down by who is affected.

comparison_rows.dimension: What each paper leaves unmeasured beyond its own time window

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper's authors state the 6-month follow-up period may be 'too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms,' so costs beyond 6 months are not captured.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper's evidence gaps state that costs beyond 6 months (longer-term or chronic trajectories) are not modeled and would require longer claims follow-up.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers stop at a 6-month window, so neither can speak to the economic burden of longer-lasting symptoms.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers explicitly say they do not measure indirect costs such as lost income, caregiving time, or productivity loss.

evidence.note: States its cost estimation 'does not include all states or indirect costs,' with indirect costs listed only as an explicit exclusion.
Lists productivity losses for patients or caregivers as explicitly not captured by the study.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers link a more severe form of the condition (disseminated Lyme disease, or hospitalized COVID-19) to a much larger direct medical cost than the milder form.

evidence.note: Reports a disseminated-to-localized per-episode cost ratio of 9.83 and a $6,138 per-episode dollar gap (2022 dollars).
Reports hospitalization cost multipliers of 3.18 for adults and 9.47 for children at 6 months (2020 dollars underlying figures).

shared_themes.theme: Both papers flag that their highest-level, most aggregated cost figures are the least broken down by demographic subgroup.

evidence.note: Reports headline costs pooled nationally and by severity/state, but not stratified by sex, age, race, ethnicity, disability, or other subgroups beyond adjustment covariates.
Reports cohort aggregate totals of up to $47 million (children) and $308 million (adults) as single pooled figures despite per-person estimates elsewhere being split by sex and age.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers limit their cost measurement window to 6 months and state that longer-term costs are not captured.

evidence.note: Authors state the 6-month follow-up may be 'too short to capture the costs for patients with persistent symptoms.'
Evidence gaps state that costs beyond 6 months are not modeled and would require longer claims follow-up.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies a specific patient out-of-pocket dollar figure per episode, something not available on the Long COVID side of this comparison.

evidence.note: Reports $188 out-of-pocket per episode overall and $401 for disseminated disease (2022 dollars), based on a 15.5% subset of cases with OOP data.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper extrapolates its findings to a multi-state annual cost range, framed explicitly as applying only to high-incidence states.

evidence.note: Extrapolates to $591,000,000-$1,050,000,000 per year in annual costs across 16 high-incidence states and DC (2022 dollars).

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper identifies a systemic gap specific to its condition: no diagnostic code for the condition existed during the study period, so cases had to be inferred rather than directly coded.

evidence.note: States the general post-COVID-19 condition code 'went into effect in October 2021, after our study period ended,' so its methodology is described as a lower bound in the setting studied.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper breaks out dollar and relative cost differences by both age subgroup and sex at the per-person level, more granular than the Lyme disease paper's per-person breakdowns provided here.

evidence.note: Reports a $2,191 six-month excess cost for adults 50-64 versus $892 for adults 18-24, and separate male ($1,764) and female ($1,530) six-month excess cost figures (2020 dollars).

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper measures indirect costs such as lost income, caregiving time, or productivity loss for the condition it covers.
Neither paper captures costs beyond its stated 6-month measurement window, so longer-term or persistent-symptom costs are unmeasured in both.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers two papers: one Lyme disease paper built from a claims-based cohort study, and one Long COVID paper built from a privately insured claims cohort from the first pandemic year. Both papers report substantial direct medical cost increases associated with the condition studied, with costs rising sharply for more severe cases (disseminated Lyme disease or hospitalized COVID-19), and both explicitly state they do not measure indirect costs like lost income or caregiving. They differ in what kind of undercounting affects their official-data figures: the Lyme disease paper relies on an unvalidated claims-based case-classification algorithm, while the Long COVID paper had no specific diagnostic code available during its study period and used a proxy method the authors call a lower bound. Only the Lyme disease paper provides a specific out-of-pocket dollar figure and a multi-state annual cost extrapolation; the Long COVID paper's aggregate dollar figures are scoped only to its own study cohort. Because each simulator was built from a single uploaded document, this is not a controlled comparison of the two conditions, and no pattern here should be generalized beyond what each paper's own figures state.
cross_analysis.limitations: This comparison is based on a small, non-random sample: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no papers covering both conditions. Real statistics confirm these sample sizes (one paper per condition, no cross or other papers), so any pattern described here reflects only these two specific documents, not the conditions in general, and this is not a controlled study.

learning_cards.headline: Ask whether severity drives Long COVID costs as sharply as Lyme disease
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper found disseminated cases cost $6138 more per episode than localized cases, a 9.83 times ratio, and adjusted disseminated patients' 6-month cost increase exceeded the overall average by $10263.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's excess cost figures are broken out by age group (children versus adults), not by a comparable severity split such as hospitalized versus non-hospitalized cases.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID researchers calculate an excess-cost gap and ratio between more severe and less severe cases, the way the Lyme disease paper did between disseminated and localized cases?

learning_cards.headline: Lyme disease paper tracked patient out-of-pocket cost; Long COVID paper did not
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports a patient out-of-pocket cost of $188 per episode.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper's figures describe excess direct medical cost to the health system but include no out-of-pocket dollar figure borne by patients.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could the Long COVID cohort data be used to calculate a comparable patient out-of-pocket cost figure alongside its existing excess cost estimates?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID paper found a sex-based cost gap; Lyme disease paper has none
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper found adult male excess cost at 6 months exceeded female excess cost by $234.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper's severity and out-of-pocket cost figures are not broken out by patient sex.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could the Lyme disease claims data be reanalyzed to see whether direct costs per episode also differ by patient sex?

learning_cards.headline: Long COVID paper split costs by age; Lyme disease paper did not
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper reports a 6-month excess direct medical cost of $1011 for children versus $1562 for adults.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper's severity cost figures (localized versus disseminated) are not broken out by patient age group.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could the Lyme disease cohort be stratified by age group to see whether the disseminated-versus-localized cost gap differs between children and adults?

learning.takeaway: Each paper measured direct medical costs from a different angle: the Lyme disease paper by disease severity and patient out-of-pocket spending, the Long COVID paper by patient age and sex; each could ask whether the other's breakdown applies to its own cohort, without assuming the answer would be the same.
